results.name: small_vs_large_target_contrast
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets <=10 minus yes rate for non-example targets >=91, pooled over all sets; observed above null means people favour small numbers as members regardless of the set more than the model predicts (below: favour large numbers).
results.code:
# name: small_vs_large_target_contrast
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets <=10 minus yes rate for non-example targets >=91, pooled over all sets; observed above null means people favour small numbers as members regardless of the set more than the model predicts (below: favour large numbers).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    mat = np.full((len(df), 4), -1)
    for j in range(4):
        mat[:, j] = pd.to_numeric(s.str[j], errors="coerce").fillna(-1).astype(int).values
    valid = mat > 0
    n = valid.sum(1)
    shown = np.any(valid & (mat == t[:, None]), 1)
    lo = np.where(valid, mat, 999).min(1)
    hi = np.where(valid, mat, -1).max(1)
    a = ~shown & (t <= 10); b = ~shown & (t >= 91)
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: powers2_set_even_nonpower_yes
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all powers of 2, yes rate for even non-power-of-2 targets; observed above null means people broaden power-of-2 sets toward 'even numbers' more than the model does (below: they hold the narrow power rule more tightly).
results.code:
# name: powers2_set_even_nonpower_yes
# description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all powers of 2, yes rate for even non-power-of-2 targets; observed above null means people broaden power-of-2 sets toward 'even numbers' more than the model does (below: they hold the narrow power rule more tightly).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    mat = np.full((len(df), 4), -1)
    for j in range(4):
        mat[:, j] = pd.to_numeric(s.str[j], errors="coerce").fillna(-1).astype(int).values
    valid = mat > 0
    n = valid.sum(1)
    shown = np.any(valid & (mat == t[:, None]), 1)
    lo = np.where(valid, mat, 999).min(1)
    hi = np.where(valid, mat, -1).max(1)
    pw = np.isin(mat, [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64])
    allp = np.all(~valid | pw, 1) & (n >= 2)
    m = allp & (t % 2 == 0) & ~np.isin(t, [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]) & ~shown
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

    mat = np.full((len(df), 4), -1)
    for j in range(4):
        mat[:, j] = pd.to_numeric(s.str[j], errors="coerce").fillna(-1).astype(int).values
    valid = mat > 0
    n = valid.sum(1)
    shown = np.any(valid & (mat == t[:, None]), 1)
    lo = np.where(valid, mat, 999).min(1)

results.name: near_outspan_generalization
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets lying 1-5 outside the [min,max] span of sets with >=2 examples; observed above null means people generalize just beyond the examples more than the model's interval/rule posterior predicts (below: they stop sharper at the edges).

def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    mat = np.full((len(df), 4), -1)
    for j in range(4):
        mat[:, j] = pd.to_numeric(s.str[j], errors="coerce").fillna(-1).astype(int).values
    valid = mat > 0
    n = valid.sum(1)
    shown = np.any(valid & (mat == t[:, None]), 1)
    lo = np.where(valid, mat, 999).min(1)

    m = (n >= 2) & ~shown & (d >= 1) & (d <= 5)

results.name: round_target_yes_nonround_sets
results.description: Among sets with no multiple-of-10 example, yes rate for multiple-of-10 targets minus yes rate for other non-example targets within 3 of a multiple of 10 (and not ending in 0); observed above null means people over-accept salient round numbers relative to the model.
results.code:
# name: round_target_yes_nonround_sets
# description: Among sets with no multiple-of-10 example, yes rate for multiple-of-10 targets minus yes rate for other non-example targets within 3 of a multiple of 10 (and not ending in 0); observed above null means people over-accept salient round numbers relative to the model.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    mat = np.full((len(df), 4), -1)
    for j in range(4):
        mat[:, j] = pd.to_numeric(s.str[j], errors="coerce").fillna(-1).astype(int).values
    valid = mat > 0
    n = valid.sum(1)
    shown = np.any(valid & (mat == t[:, None]), 1)
    lo = np.where(valid, mat, 999).min(1)
    hi = np.where(valid, mat, -1).max(1)
    anyround = np.any(valid & (mat % 10 == 0), 1)
    base = ~anyround & ~shown
    tm = t % 10
    a = base & (tm == 0)
    b = base & (tm != 0) & ((tm <= 3) | (tm >= 7))
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: prime_set_prime_vs_odd_composite
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all odd primes, yes rate for non-example prime targets minus yes rate for odd composite targets; observed below null means people fail to distinguish primes from other odd numbers as sharply as the model predicts (above: they discriminate more).
results.code:
# name: prime_set_prime_vs_odd_composite
# description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all odd primes, yes rate for non-example prime targets minus yes rate for odd composite targets; observed below null means people fail to distinguish primes from other odd numbers as sharply as the model predicts (above: they discriminate more).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    mat = np.full((len(df), 4), -1)
    for j in range(4):
        mat[:, j] = pd.to_numeric(s.str[j], errors="coerce").fillna(-1).astype(int).values
    valid = mat > 0
    n = valid.sum(1)
    shown = np.any(valid & (mat == t[:, None]), 1)
    lo = np.where(valid, mat, 999).min(1)
    hi = np.where(valid, mat, -1).max(1)
    P = np.array([k for k in range(2, 101) if all(k % a for a in range(2, int(k ** 0.5) + 1))])
    isp = np.isin(mat, P) & (mat % 2 == 1)
    allp = np.all(~valid | isp, 1) & (n >= 2)
    tp = np.isin(t, P)
    a = allp & tp & ~shown
    b = allp & ~tp & (t % 2 == 1) & (t > 1)
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: wide_sparse_interior_yes
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples spanning >=30, yes rate for non-example targets strictly inside the span; observed below null means people do not fill the gaps of wide sparse sets as the model's ranges/rules imply (above: they fill gaps more).
results.code:

def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    mat = np.full((len(df), 4), -1)

results.name: units_digit_shared_contrast
results.description: Among sets with >=2 examples whose examples do not all share a last digit, yes rate for non-example targets sharing a last digit with some example minus yes rate for targets sharing none; observed above null means people use loose last-digit similarity the model lacks.
results.code:
# name: units_digit_shared_contrast
# description: Among sets with >=2 examples whose examples do not all share a last digit, yes rate for non-example targets sharing a last digit with some example minus yes rate for targets sharing none; observed above null means people use loose last-digit similarity the model lacks.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",")
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    mat = np.full((len(df), 4), -1)
    for j in range(4):
        mat[:, j] = pd.to_numeric(s.str[j], errors="coerce").fillna(-1).astype(int).values
    valid = mat > 0
    n = valid.sum(1)
    shown = np.any(valid & (mat == t[:, None]), 1)
    lo = np.where(valid, mat, 999).min(1)
    hi = np.where(valid, mat, -1).max(1)
    u = np.where(valid, mat % 10, -1)
    same_end = np.all(~valid | (u == u[:, :1]), 1)
    share = np.any(valid & (u == (t % 10)[:, None]), 1)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~same_end & ~shown
    a = base & share; b = base & ~share
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
